title: Joining crochet squares: strips versus all-at-once
subtitle: Comparing the two main construction orders for assembling a blanket from individual squares
excerpt: When assembling a blanket from individual squares, the construction order is a practical decision that affects how many seams you handle at once and whether the joins are consistent across the piece. The two approaches are: joining into strips first and then joining the strips, or joining all squares in one pass across the full fabric at once.
sourceNotes: Pauline Turner, How to Crochet (HarperCollins). Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing).

glossaryTerms.definition: A blanket assembly method where individual squares are first joined into long strips and the strips are then joined to each other. Each seam is a single long join rather than a series of short ones.

A joining method in which squares are held with wrong sides together and a row of slip stitches or single crochet is worked along the adjoining edges, producing a ridge on one side (the right side or wrong side depending on which you prefer).

content.text: and all-at-once joining are the two standard construction orders for blankets made from individual squares. Strip joining handles each seam as a long single join from top to bottom, then joins the finished strips side by side. All-at-once joining works a single seam across the full width of the blanket, row by row from top to bottom. Both produce the same finished fabric; the difference is how much you are handling at once and which errors are easiest to catch.

items.name: All squares blocked to the same dimensions before joining
items.note: This is the single most important preparation step. Joining unblocked squares produces a rippling, uneven fabric that is very difficult to block flat after assembly.

items.name: Yarn for joining
items.note: Either the same yarn as the squares, or a contrast colour for a decorative seam effect

items.name: Tapestry needle
items.note: For weaving in ends at each join

content.text: Lay all squares out in the finished arrangement and number or photograph the position of each one before starting. Once joining begins, it is easy to lose track of orientation.
Join each column of squares into a strip. Hold two squares with right sides together and work a
along the shared edge: slip stitch or double crochet through both outer edges. Fasten off and add the next square.
Fasten off at the end of each column seam. Weave in the ends before adding the next square.

Once all columns are joined, join the columns to each other: hold two adjacent columns right sides together and work a flat join from one end to the other. This is a long seam, so mark the joining point every 20 cm with a stitch marker to prevent drift.
Lay the full arrangement of squares out flat. Join the first row of squares left to right: hold each pair right sides together and work the flat join. The first row of joined squares is now a strip.
Join the second row of squares to each other in the same way, then join the bottom edge of the first strip to the top edge of the second strip.

Repeat for each row. The full blanket grows from top to bottom. The advantage is that you can check the layout and orientation of each row before you join it, and alignment errors are easier to catch because the growing blanket is in front of you.

items.symptom: The join ridge is visible and prominent on the right side
items.cause: The squares were held wrong sides together for the flat join, which places the ridge on the right side.
items.fix: Both are valid: some patterns intentionally use the ridge as a decorative element. If you want the ridge hidden, hold the squares right sides together so the ridge falls on the wrong side.

items.symptom: The blanket is rippling and does not lie flat after assembly
items.cause: Individual squares were not blocked to the same dimensions before joining, so different-sized squares are pulling against each other.
items.fix: Wet-block the assembled blanket. The moisture allows the joins to relax. Pin the blanket to the correct overall dimensions and leave to dry. This often fixes moderate rippling.

items.symptom: Corner junctions where four squares meet are bulky
items.cause: Four seam ridges converge at each corner junction.
items.fix: At corner junctions, work a slip stitch into the junction point from both directions rather than working several stitches through all four layers. This distributes the bulk.

content.text: A 4-square sampler (2 by 2) assembled by both methods shows the difference immediately. Try both: join-as-you-go directly into the last round of the square produces the flattest corner junctions of all the joining methods and is worth learning for any project where the joins need to be nearly invisible.
